   As Zacharia began outlining her plans for the job, Trump’s senior adviser Jason Miller knocked on the door. Vice President JD Vance wanted to chat. Zacharia never returned—to the interview, nor the job.

   Philip Wegmann, Kara Voght and Marianne LeVine chronicle the difficult circumstances surrounding her appointment and the extraordinary moment her tenure ended .

       2. TODAY’S HEADLINES   • Trump is halting implementation of most of the sanctions that were to be imposed on Russia under a bipartisan bill he signed last month.

   • A broad tech selloff capped Wall Street’s worst week since June , as concerns over AI investments, Chinese chipmaking advances and inflation rattled investors.

   • Lawyers for Rep. Ilhan Omar sent a letter to federal prosecutors challenging the legality of a search of her home earlier this week and asking for the immediate return of all property seized.

   • The cancellation of Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution followed days of internal debate triggered by the defense secretary’s announcement, which officials in Washington said came as a surprise.

   • Iranian support, from targeting help to training, has helped the Houthis mount the most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies.

   • Police said a teacher and a father heroically intervened to stop a 16-year-old shooter in this week’s attack on an Oregon elementary school, saving others’ lives.

       3. FROM THE MARKETS   • PepsiCo used to embody everything investors prized in a stock. That reputation is fading, writes columnist David Wainer .

   • Elon Musk’s flying Tesla Roadster signals a retreat from designing cars for everyday drivers . Its unveiling underscores his broader pivot toward robotics, as Chinese brands challenge established Western automakers, writes Tim Higgins.

But when those assets reach the grandchildren, things can get messy. Today, many cousins lack the close relationships that allow them to cooperate as business partners, which is what they become the moment they jointly inherit an asset. Harvard Business School’s Christina Wing calls this the “cousin problem.” Drawing on her work advising families, she explains why inheritances can become a source of resentment —and what families can do to prevent disputes before they begin.

   5.   Blue Owl’s founders promised a comeback, but its stock hasn’t budged.   Back in March, when Blue Owl found itself at the center of the backlash against private credit, staff were told, “We’re going to emerge stronger from this storm.” But clients have continued to ask to withdraw their money, and its stock recently dipped to near all-time lows—bad news for employees’ stock-based pay. Equipped with advanced perception systems that give way to merging cars and detect hazards early, these autonomous vehicles are suited to handle repetitive depot-to-depot routes known as the middle mile. We take you onto the highway to see how driverless freight could reshape logistics as major companies face rising shipping costs and demand.

       7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND   • Saturday: Trump is scheduled to speak in Kentucky. The Golden State Valkyries face the Atlanta Dream in Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. In baseball, the Tampa Bay Rays take on the Cleveland Guardians in Game 4 of the American League Championship Series.

   • Sunday: China will release third-quarter GDP figures. The IMF and World Bank’s annual meetings conclude in Bangkok. A full slate of NFL games kicks off, including a matchup in London.

As demand softens in traditional luxury strongholds like China and the Middle East, the U.S. is emerging as a rare bright spot for the brand. Rather than making wealthy shoppers go on a pilgrimage to a store in Manhattan or Beverly Hills, Hermès is chasing customers by meeting them where they are: wealthy suburbs and smaller American cities like Nashville and Austin.

AND FINALLY…   A luxury watch is becoming the ultimate icebreaker for women in business.   A growing number of women are saying that becoming a watch enthusiast has unlocked an unexpected workplace advantage. A comment about a timepiece gives them an entree into conversations traditionally dominated by men—helping build rapport, gain social capital and close deals.

       10. BEYOND THE NEWSROOM   • Opinion: The progressive “abundance” movement is getting an election test in California, where the climate lobby and unions have come out swinging against a ballot initiative that would accelerate permitting.

Katie Zacharia Projected Confidence. Less Than an Hour Later, She Was Out.
 
Plus, Ilhan Omar challenges the legality of a search of her home, and the hidden problem with passing down a family inheritance
 
 
JULIA DEMAREE NIKHINSON/AP
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Katie Zacharia was just five days into her job as White House press secretary when she sat down with our reporters on Friday. Despite a tumultuous week, she projected calm, touting her close relationship with President Trump and expressing confidence in her press team.

 

“There are no staffing changes that are happening,” she told the reporters.

 

As Zacharia began outlining her plans for the job, Trump’s senior adviser Jason Miller knocked on the door. Vice President JD Vance wanted to chat. Zacharia never returned—to the interview, nor the job.

 

Philip Wegmann, Kara Voght and Marianne LeVine chronicle the difficult circumstances surrounding her appointment and the extraordinary moment her tenure ended.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Trump is halting implementation of most of the sanctions that were to be imposed on Russia under a bipartisan bill he signed last month.

 

• A broad tech selloff capped Wall Street’s worst week since June, as concerns over AI investments, Chinese chipmaking advances and inflation rattled investors.

 

• Lawyers for Rep. Ilhan Omar sent a letter to federal prosecutors challenging the legality of a search of her home earlier this week and asking for the immediate return of all property seized.

 

• The cancellation of Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution followed days of internal debate triggered by the defense secretary’s announcement, which officials in Washington said came as a surprise.

 

• Iranian support, from targeting help to training, has helped the Houthis mount the most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies.

 

• Police said a teacher and a father heroically intervened to stop a 16-year-old shooter in this week’s attack on an Oregon elementary school, saving others’ lives.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• PepsiCo used to embody everything investors prized in a stock. That reputation is fading, writes columnist David Wainer.

 

• Elon Musk’s flying Tesla Roadster signals a retreat from designing cars for everyday drivers. Its unveiling underscores his broader pivot toward robotics, as Chinese brands challenge established Western automakers, writes Tim Higgins.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The inheritance problem that can tear families apart.

 

Passing down a family business or vacation home might seem like a generous gift to future generations. But when those assets reach the grandchildren, things can get messy. Today, many cousins lack the close relationships that allow them to cooperate as business partners, which is what they become the moment they jointly inherit an asset. Harvard Business School’s Christina Wing calls this the “cousin problem.” Drawing on her work advising families, she explains why inheritances can become a source of resentment—and what families can do to prevent disputes before they begin.

 

5.

 

Blue Owl’s founders promised a comeback, but its stock hasn’t budged.

 

Back in March, when Blue Owl found itself at the center of the backlash against private credit, staff were told, “We’re going to emerge stronger from this storm.” But clients have continued to ask to withdraw their money, and its stock recently dipped to near all-time lows—bad news for employees’ stock-based pay. In search of growth, the firm’s leadership has pivoted toward a huge bet on financing and building AI data centers, reports Matt Wirz.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

The most polite trucker in America is a driverless 18-wheeler.

 
 
DREW DUCOTE FOR WSJ
 

Driverless trucks are on the interstate in Texas and can do almost everything a human truck driver does, except honk. Equipped with advanced perception systems that give way to merging cars and detect hazards early, these autonomous vehicles are suited to handle repetitive depot-to-depot routes known as the middle mile. We take you onto the highway to see how driverless freight could reshape logistics as major companies face rising shipping costs and demand.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND

 

• Saturday: Trump is scheduled to speak in Kentucky. The Golden State Valkyries face the Atlanta Dream in Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. In baseball, the Tampa Bay Rays take on the Cleveland Guardians in Game 4 of the American League Championship Series.

 

• Sunday: China will release third-quarter GDP figures. The IMF and World Bank’s annual meetings conclude in Bangkok. A full slate of NFL games kicks off, including a matchup in London.

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
15%
 

That is the revenue growth Hermès saw in the Americas during the first half of this year. As demand softens in traditional luxury strongholds like China and the Middle East, the U.S. is emerging as a rare bright spot for the brand. Rather than making wealthy shoppers go on a pilgrimage to a store in Manhattan or Beverly Hills, Hermès is chasing customers by meeting them where they are: wealthy suburbs and smaller American cities like Nashville and Austin.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

A luxury watch is becoming the ultimate icebreaker for women in business.

 

A growing number of women are saying that becoming a watch enthusiast has unlocked an unexpected workplace advantage. A comment about a timepiece gives them an entree into conversations traditionally dominated by men—helping build rapport, gain social capital and close deals.
